section: I. Comprehension – Section One: Reading Passage I
prompt:
[Reading Passage I — Homelessness and Personal Responsibility]
1. Homeless people are everywhere—on the street, in public buildings, on the evening news and at the corner parking lot. You can hardly step out of your house these days without meeting some haggard character who asks you for a cigarette or begs for 'a little change'. The homeless are not just constant symbols of wasted lives and social programs—they have become a danger to public safety.
2. What is the root of the homeless problem? Everyone seems to have a scapegoat. Advocates of the homeless blame government policy; politicians blame the legal system; the courts blame the bureaucratic infrastructure; the Democrats blame the Republicans and the Republicans blame the Democrats. The public also blames the economy, drugs, the 'poverty cycle', and 'the breakdown of society'. With all this finger-pointing, the group most responsible for the homeless being the way they are received the least blame. That group is the homeless themselves.
3. How can I say this? For the past two years I have worked with the homeless, volunteering at the Salvation Army and at a soup kitchen in Austin, Texas. I have led a weekly chapel service, served food, listened, counseled, given time and money, and shared their struggles. I have seen their response to troubles, and though I would rather report otherwise, many of them seem to have chosen the lifestyles they lead. They are unwilling to do the things necessary to overcome their circumstances. They must bear the greatest part of the blame for their manifold troubles.
4. Let me qualify what I just said. Not everyone who finds himself out of a job and in the street is there because he/she wants to be. Some are victims of tragic circumstances. I met many exhausted, sensible people during my time working with Austin's homeless: the single father struggling to earn his bread and be a role model for his children; the woman who fled a good job in another city to escape an abusive husband; the well-educated young man who had his world turned upside down by divorce and a layoff. These people deserve every effort to help them back on their feet.
5. But they are not the real problem. They are usually off the streets and resuming normal lives within a period of weeks or months. Even while 'down on their luck', they are responsible citizens, working in the shelters and applying for jobs. They are homeless, true, but only temporarily, because they are eager to reorganize their lives.
6. For every person temporarily homeless, though, there are many who are chronically so. Whether because of mental illness, alcoholism, poor education, drug addiction, or simply laziness, these homeless are content to remain as they are. In many cases they choose the streets. They enjoy the freedom and consider begging a minor inconvenience. They know they can always get a job for a day or two for food, cigarettes and alcohol. The sophisticated among them have learned to use the system for what it is worth and figure out that a trip through the welfare line is less trouble than a steady job. In a society that has mastered dodging responsibility, these homeless prefer a life of no responsibility at all.
Source: Critical Thinking, Thoughtful Writing: A Rhetoric with Readings by Chaffee, J. U.S.A. (1999), pp. 374–375.

None of those in the street deserves any effort to help them back on their feet.
A woman fleeing an abusive husband is right away homeless.
Everyone who finds themselves out of a job is homeless.

explanation: Present regret about an unreal past situation is expressed with 'wish (present) + past perfect'—and since the speaker would have received the advice, passive past perfect ('wish I had been advised') is required (A).

explanation: Questions about general life experience up to the present use the present perfect tense ('Have + subject + ever + past participle'). The past participle of the main verb 'have' (in 'have a chance') is 'had'—giving 'Have you ever had...' (C).

unit: Unit 5: Grammar and Usage (Conditionals, Tenses, Modals & Connectors)
prompt: Question 43: The road project ______________ by the construction company next year.
explanation: The time marker 'next year' requires a future form. Option A ('will be completing') is active, B ('was completed') is past tense, and C ('will completed') omits 'be.' Option D ('will be complete') is grammatically well-formed.

section: II. Language Focus / Grammar
unit: Unit 5: Grammar and Usage (Conditionals, Tenses, Modals & Connectors)
prompt: Question 44: If I had enough money, I ______________ schools with elevators for visually impaired children.
explanation: This is a Type 2 (Second) Conditional sentence describing a hypothetical present situation ('If I had enough money' — simple past in the if-clause). The main clause must use 'would + base verb' ('would build', Option B; note: the source booklet's explanation explicitly confirms 'would build' as correct despite a typo in its answer letter).

section: II. Language Focus / Grammar
unit: Unit 5: Grammar and Usage (Conditionals, Tenses, Modals & Connectors)
prompt: Question 45: Next year this time, I ______________ the freshman program.
explanation: The future time expression 'Next year this time' signals an action that will be completed before or by a specific point in the future, requiring the future perfect tense: 'will have almost completed' (A).

section: II. Language Focus / Grammar
unit: Unit 5: Grammar and Usage (Conditionals, Tenses, Modals & Connectors)
prompt: Question 46: This year's examination is as good as the one given last year, ______________?
explanation: A positive statement with the present tense linking verb 'is' ('This year's examination is...') takes a negative question tag with the same auxiliary and pronoun: 'isn't it?' (C).

section: II. Language Focus / Grammar
unit: Unit 5: Grammar and Usage (Conditionals, Tenses, Modals & Connectors)
prompt: Question 47: I met the girl ______________ phone number I was asking for.
explanation: The relative pronoun must show possession before the noun phrase 'phone number' (i.e., the girl's phone number). 'Whose' (B) is the possessive relative pronoun.

section: II. Language Focus / Grammar
unit: Unit 5: Grammar and Usage (Conditionals, Tenses, Modals & Connectors)
prompt: Question 48: When you acknowledge people's contribution to your work, you need not refer ______________ his/her name.
explanation: The verb 'refer' always takes the dependent preposition 'to' ('refer to someone/something') when meaning to mention or cite (A).

section: II. Language Focus / Grammar
unit: Unit 5: Grammar and Usage (Conditionals, Tenses, Modals & Connectors)
prompt: Question 49: ______________ listening ______________ reading are important academic skills students need to develop.
explanation: The plural verb 'are' and the meaning that both skills are essential academic competencies require the inclusive correlative conjunction pair 'Both ... and' (C). 'Either/or' and 'Neither/nor' would take a singular verb ('is') with singular gerunds.

section: II. Language Focus / Grammar
topic: Verb Tenses / Present Simple for Habitual Actions
unit: Unit 5: Grammar and Usage (Conditionals, Tenses, Modals & Connectors)
prompt: Question 50: He ______________ his children to school five days a week.
explanation: 'Five days a week' indicates a regular, habitual routine, which requires the simple present tense. With the third-person singular subject 'He,' the verb takes '-s': 'drives' (A).

section: II. Language Focus / Grammar
unit: Unit 5: Grammar and Usage (Conditionals, Tenses, Modals & Connectors)
prompt: Question 51: My father is not ______________ old ______________ yours; he is only 53 years old.
explanation: Comparisons of equality or inequality with an adjective ('old') use the correlative structure 'as + adjective + as' ('not as old as yours', D).

section: II. Language Focus / Grammar
topic: Adverbial Clauses of Result / 'such a...that' vs. 'so...that'
unit: Unit 5: Grammar and Usage (Conditionals, Tenses, Modals & Connectors)
prompt: Question 52: Lojo is ______________ tall girl ______________ she can easily touch the ceiling of her classroom.
explanation: When an adjective + singular countable noun ('tall girl') precedes the result clause, the structure 'such a + adjective + singular countable noun + that' is required: 'such a tall girl that...' (B).

section: II. Language Focus / Grammar
unit: Unit 5: Grammar and Usage (Conditionals, Tenses, Modals & Connectors)
prompt: Question 53: Some students did well on the last week's English test, ______________ others scored unsatisfactory marks. I am designing an action research to study the case.
explanation: 'Whereas' (C) is a subordinating conjunction of contrast used to compare two direct opposites ('Some students did well... whereas others scored unsatisfactory marks'). 'Despite' (B) is a preposition and cannot join two finite clauses directly.

section: II. Language Focus / Grammar
unit: Unit 5: Grammar and Usage (Conditionals, Tenses, Modals & Connectors)
prompt: Question 54: My English teacher ______________ me repeat the correct answer ten times.
explanation: The causative verb 'make' in the active voice is followed by an object + bare infinitive without 'to' ('made me repeat'). 'Wanted' (A), 'forced' (B), and 'told' (C) all require a 'to'-infinitive ('to repeat').

section: II. Language Focus / Grammar
unit: Unit 5: Grammar and Usage (Conditionals, Tenses, Modals & Connectors)
prompt: Question 55: My history teacher asked me ______________ (Direct question: 'What is your nationality?')
explanation: In reported questions, question word order (verb-subject) shifts to statement word order (subject-verb), the pronoun 'your' shifts to 'my,' and no question mark is used. Options B, C, and D retain inverted question word order ('is/was + subject'), making Option A ('what my nationality is') the only grammatically valid indirect question structure.

section: II. Language Focus / Grammar
unit: Unit 5: Grammar and Usage (Conditionals, Tenses, Modals & Connectors)
prompt: Question 56: You ______________ go to bed before midnight if you have the habit of getting up late.
explanation: 'Will not' (A) expresses a predictable future/habitual consequence in a first-conditional structure: if you habitually wake up late, you will not go to bed early (before midnight). 'Must not' (prohibition) does not fit.

section: II. Language Focus / Grammar
topic: Time Conjunctions / Adverbial Clauses of Time
unit: Unit 5: Grammar and Usage (Conditionals, Tenses, Modals & Connectors)
prompt: Question 57: You will start running ______________ the bell rings. Otherwise, you will be disqualified from the competition.
explanation: According to the exam key, 'while' (B) is selected to indicate simultaneous immediacy (starting at the very moment the bell is ringing). Note that 'during' (C) is a preposition and cannot precede a clause, and 'till' (A) means 'up to the time.'

section: II. Language Focus / Grammar
topic: Degree Modifiers / 'too + adjective + for + object + to-infinitive'
unit: Unit 5: Grammar and Usage (Conditionals, Tenses, Modals & Connectors)
prompt: Question 58: The afternoon sun is ______________ hot for school children ______________ play outside. They had better stay in their class.
explanation: The correlative pattern 'too + adjective + (for someone) + to-infinitive' ('too hot for school children to play outside') expresses excess that prevents an action (B).

section: II. Language Focus / Grammar
unit: Unit 5: Grammar and Usage (Conditionals, Tenses, Modals & Connectors)
prompt: Question 59: The lady ______________ next to our English teacher is my mother's close friend.
explanation: 'Sitting' (A) forms a present participial phrase (reduced relative clause from 'who is sitting') modifying 'The lady.' Using a finite verb like 'sits' (D) or 'sat' (C) without 'who' would create a double-verb syntax error.

section: II. Language Focus / Grammar
unit: Unit 5: Grammar and Usage (Conditionals, Tenses, Modals & Connectors)
prompt: Question 60: Unlike my friends, who dislike drinking coffee, I ______________ go to bed at night without coffee.
explanation: The introductory phrase 'Unlike my friends, who dislike drinking coffee' sets up a contrast: the speaker loves coffee. Because the sentence ends with 'without coffee,' the negative adverb 'never' ('never go to bed... without coffee' = always drink coffee before bed) is required to maintain the contrast (A).

section: II. Language Focus / Grammar
topic: Cause & Effect Verbs / 'leads to' vs. 'arises from'
unit: Unit 5: Grammar and Usage (Conditionals, Tenses, Modals & Connectors)
prompt: Question 61: Committing corruption ______________ life imprisonment in several countries in the world.
explanation: 'Leads to' (D) means 'results in' or 'brings about as a consequence/punishment.' Committing corruption causes/results in life imprisonment. 'Arises from' (B) reverses the cause-and-effect relationship.

section: II. Language Focus / Grammar
topic: Adverbs of Degree & Frequency / Negative Adverbs ('scarcely')
unit: Unit 5: Grammar and Usage (Conditionals, Tenses, Modals & Connectors)
prompt: Question 62: I always have much work to do; that is why I ______________ have time to listen to music.
explanation: Because the speaker always has a heavy workload, they almost never have free time. 'Scarcely' (C), meaning 'hardly' or 'almost never,' conveys this near-absence of free time.
